events.text: A cloud-barge with no banner puts in at your landing at dusk, and a single passenger steps off who has the bearing of a drawn sword. {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}. Your name was written under theirs on the Ten's list, once, and then you struck it out. "A duel to the end," they say, civilly. "Not for the list. For the ending."

choices.text: Name the White Stairs as the ground and draw

effects.log: You name the stairs. They bow, and you are both climbing before the barge has finished rocking.

choices.text: Refuse, and offer them a seat and a cup

effects.log: You offer the cup. They look at it a long time, and set it down untouched, and the barge casts off.

events.text: On the Jade Court's morning roll there is a notice in a hand you recognise: {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}, challenges you to a final meeting on the isle of their choosing, three nights hence. Court custom lets you decline. Court custom also notes, mildly, how many who declined were not heard of again at any gathering of consequence.

choices.text: Accept, and go early to read the ground

effects.log: You arrive a night before. The isle is bare and swept, and there is a fresh lamp waiting for you on a flat stone.

choices.text: Decline in writing, and take the Court's mild note on the chin

effects.log: The Court records your refusal in tidy characters. The word beside it is "prudent" or "cowardly". It is hard to read.

choices.text: Send a letter instead, asking what they would take to let it lie

effects.log: The answer comes back in one line: "A ruling." You are not sure whose.

events.text: You wake to find a single white plum blossom on your pillow, which is the old mark of {gj9_name} when they have decided something. {gj9_title}, still a name that makes the Court rise. They are waiting on the cloud outside your window, sitting very straight. They say, "I did not come to take it back. I came to finish it."

choices.text: Rise, take up your sword, and meet them on the cloud

effects.log: You step out onto the cloud as onto a floor. It holds, because both of you insist that it should.

choices.text: Tell them it is finished already, and mean it

effects.log: They look at you, and for a moment the old face shows. Then it is gone, and they are walking away on the cloud.

events.text: A line of ink in the margin of your own diary, in someone else's hand: "At the Pavilion of Seven Rains, at dawn. Alone." It is signed {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}. You search your hall for the intruder and find only a cup of tea, gone cold, poured for two. Only one cup has been drunk from.

choices.text: Go to the Pavilion at dawn, as written

effects.log: The Pavilion is empty until the first light, and then it is not. Both of you bow before anything else happens.

choices.text: Burn the diary page, and stay at home

effects.log: You burn it. At dawn the rains come to the Pavilion alone, and no one is there to watch them.

choices.text: Go earlier than they expect, and wait

effects.log: You are first. When they arrive and see you, they smile. It is almost a relief to them.

events.text: {gj9_name} does not get up. The cloud under the two of you slowly goes quiet. {gj9_title}, and it came to this on a clear morning, with the tea still warm in the next room. The Court's runners are on their way; so is the news. You stand a while longer on the cloud, listening for an old voice, and there is none.

choices.text: Close their eyes, and say the old words

effects.log: You do it properly. A little of the weight lifts, as if the old words were a coin laid in a hand.

choices.text: Take the sword, and leave the rest

effects.log: The sword is light and very cold. You will carry it a long time, and it will not feel like a prize.

events.text: They lie with their face to the sky. The Court's Ministry of Rites will have its say about the ceremony, and the Ten will have an empty chair, and the isles will call you something by nightfall. A white plum petal drifts down onto their coat from nowhere. You could swear you smell tea.

choices.text: Carry them down to the lower isles for burial

effects.log: They are buried under a plain stone, in a village that sweeps it each year. You keep the village's name.

choices.text: Leave the body to the Court, and walk away

effects.log: The Court takes it with proper ceremony. You are not asked to the ceremony, and are, on the whole, glad.

events.text: {gj9_name} is buried on a lower isle above a village that still sweeps the grave each spring. The stone says only {gj9_title}. White paper streamers move in no wind. In your sleeve the Corpse-Commanding Talisman is warm, and the bell, which has not rung for three years, is trying to ring on its own.

choices.text: Write the yellow script and ring the bell

effects.log: You write the script. The ground turns, once, like a sleeper, and the grass above it flattens.

choices.text: Leave before the villagers see you

effects.log: You leave quietly. Behind you the streamers stop moving all at once, like something that has been told to wait.

choices.text: Burn incense, and seal the grave for good

effects.log: The incense burns straight. You lay a stone on the stone, and the bell in your sleeve goes quiet and cold.

events.text: A cloud-barge carries you, unasked, to the isle where {gj9_name} was laid. {gj9_title}. The ferryman will not meet your eye. The grave is a clean little mound with a single plum tree growing from it, which should not be there, because it was not planted. The bell sings once, low, from your sleeve.

choices.text: Cut the yellow script by the plum tree and ring

effects.log: The tree sheds all its blossoms at once, in a long breath, and the mound begins to rise.

choices.text: Turn the barge around and go home

effects.log: The ferryman is visibly relieved. The plum tree watches the barge go, and does not bloom again that year.

choices.text: Plant a second stone, and say the closing words

effects.log: You say them slowly. The plum tree gives a faint sigh and holds still. The bell is quiet from that day.

events.text: At the hour of the ox the bell on your wall speaks without a hand: one note, cold and very clear, and a direction. It points to the grave of {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}. You can feel the old art stirring there, patient, a sleeper turning toward warm voices. The yellow script you carry curls very slightly at the edge, as paper does near a flame.

choices.text: Go to the grave, and answer the bell

effects.log: You go. At the grave you do not speak a word; you only write, and ring. The earth listens.

choices.text: Muffle the bell with a wet cloth and bury it a while

effects.log: You bury the bell in the garden. For a week the herbs above it lean toward the north, and then they stop.

choices.text: Take salt, a lamp and an oath to the grave, and close it

effects.log: The salt makes a ring, the lamp burns steady, and the oath holds. The grave sleeps on, undisturbed.

events.text: What rose from the grave of {gj9_name} did not bend its knees to rise. It stands in your courtyard, taller than a mortal should be, wrapped in yellow script, with a face composed in an old courtesy. {gj9_title}. The bell has only to ring and it will turn. Your disciples, who know better, have bolted their doors and are praying through the walls.

choices.text: Ring once, softly, to learn if it still obeys

effects.log: It turns, with a creak like a gate in cold air, and bows. It has done this before, to better masters.

choices.text: Have a lamp lit at its feet and leave it standing till dawn

effects.log: It stands till dawn without a tremor. You do not sleep, and neither, in a way, does it.

events.text: The first night, it only stands. The second, it takes three steps and stops. On the third it turns toward the east, where a long white ridge of cloud marks the road to the Ten's old hall, and stays there until the bell makes it look away. {gj9_name}, you think. {gj9_title}. It remembers something, even now.

choices.text: Ring it to the west, away from the ridge

effects.log: It goes west, jerky and obedient, and the whole isle breathes out. You hold the bell harder than you meant to.

choices.text: Sit with it a while in the quiet, and ask nothing

effects.log: It does not answer. But for the length of one lamp's burning the air in the yard is a little less cold.

events.text: The bell rings by itself at midnight, three times. When you reach the coffin the lid is on the floor and {gj9_name} stands in the courtyard, facing the road, unbent. It is not waiting for your bell. It is remembering the way to somewhere, {gj9_title}. The yellow script has begun to curl at its edges like a leaf in fire.

choices.text: Ring the bell and hold it with your whole will

effects.log: You ring and ring. The script uncurls, the arms drop, and it turns back to you like a tide.

choices.text: Paste the sealing script on its back and lay it down for good

effects.log: The sealing script goes on. It stands a moment, then bows, then lies down by itself.

choices.text: Open the gate, and let it go where it is going

effects.log: It goes through the gate without turning. Somewhere along the cloud road a lamp is lit for it, or you imagine so.

events.text: Your bell is cracked. Hairline, but the note is wrong, like a voice carrying a thing it can no longer hold. {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}, has begun to move in the night on its own, a step at a time, always toward the Court. Two nights ago it reached the gate of the isle. This morning it is standing in the doorway of your bedroom.

choices.text: Mend the bell with fresh script and ring it hard

effects.log: The new script blazes and drinks. The bell clears. The figure at the door steps back one pace and bows its head.

choices.text: Stand in the doorway yourself and say the closing words

effects.log: You say them. It listens, wholly still, to the very end. Then it kneels, folded neat as paper.

choices.text: Step aside from the doorway, and let it walk

effects.log: It walks past you. The cloud road bends, once, to take it. After a time you cannot hear the steps.

events.text: Birds will not roost on your isle any more. The tea goes bitter in an hour. The Great stands in the cold herb garden at night, among the frost, and there is frost on the ground only where it has stood. {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}. Your script on its forehead has faded to the colour of old paper. It will not stay on much longer.

choices.text: Rewrite the script in fresh cinnabar ink and bind it again

effects.log: The ink is cinnabar and not what it sounds like. The Great shudders, and the frost goes out of the garden.

choices.text: Sing the closing chant, and lay it in the ground yourself

effects.log: You dig the grave with your own hands. It lies down in it, and you cover it, and neither of you speaks.

choices.text: Cut the old script from its brow, and let it be what it was

effects.log: The script comes away. It stands a moment as itself, and gives a nod that is nearly a bow.

events.text: Notices hang in the cloud-barge ports now, under a line in vermilion: whoever raised {gj9_name}, once of the Ten Immortals Under Cloud, has desecrated the Court's own dead. Tonight a band of the Jade Court's Wardens and three priests of the Dao Shrine surround your landing, lanterns up, and ask for the Great in the name of the Ministry of Rites.

choices.text: Stand your ground beside the Great, bell in hand

effects.log: You stand. The Wardens waver, and the priests recite, and the Great does not move. After a long hour they withdraw.

choices.text: Slip away by the lower stair and let them search an empty hall

effects.log: You slip away. They find an empty hall and one cold bell, which they dutifully carry off.

events.text: A letter, unsigned, from the Court's old Archivist: they know. The Ten have met in closed session, and a Ministry runner is already on a cloud-barge with a writ and a writ-bearer. It is kindly written and entirely clear. "I would not," the Archivist adds, in the margin, "like to see how you answer it."

choices.text: Receive the writ-bearer openly, and argue your case

effects.log: You argue it. The writ-bearer is polite and unmoved, but he leaves without the Great, and with a great deal to report.

choices.text: Send the Great into the lower isles and clear your landing

effects.log: The Great goes down with a chain of your disciples. The writ-bearer finds your landing swept, and blinks.

events.text: The tea-seller at the lowest landing will not take your coin. She says, in a very low voice, that three Wardens were by, asking about a figure in yellow script on a certain isle. She does not ask if it is true. She presses a packet of dried plums into your hand and says she has seen worse things end well.

choices.text: Go home and prepare your hall for a visit

effects.log: You prepare. When they come, they find the hall in order and the Great at rest, and an argument is made on solid ground.

choices.text: Move the Great at night, and shut the gate

effects.log: You move it by night, in a covered barge, at an unfashionable hour. The Wardens come at dawn to a locked gate and a swept yard.

events.text: You wake to find {gj9_name} standing over your bed, perfectly still, in the stance that began the last form of its art. It has never moved without the bell. The stance is beautiful. {gj9_title}. It is also, very faintly, aimed at you, and the room has gone as quiet as the cloud-sea at midnight.

choices.text: Watch the form to its end, without moving

effects.log: It finishes the form. It is the best you have ever seen, and when it is done, it bows to you as to an equal.

choices.text: Speak the closing words and lay the figure to rest

effects.log: You say them. The figure unbends slowly, as if grateful for the cue, and is still.

events.text: The bell has not rung, but the Great speaks. One word, perhaps two, from a throat that has not breathed in years: a name, the one you do not use. {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}, looks at you with something that is nearly recognition. "You," it says, and then something about a promise made on the White Stairs, in a year you cannot remember.

choices.text: Ask what the promise was, and wait for an answer

effects.log: It does not answer. But it holds your eye a long moment, and you have the oddest feeling of being forgiven.

choices.text: Say the closing words before it can say more

effects.log: You say them, quickly, a little ashamed. It bows its head, and the room fills with the smell of rain.

events.text: In the cold small hours a voice you almost know says, from the courtyard, "Do you remember the second move?" It is {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}, in the voice of the one who taught that move to you in a lamplit hall, a long time ago. There is no malice in it. It sounds like a question asked across a table.

choices.text: Answer, and show the second move

effects.log: You show it. The Great mirrors you, slowly, without a sound, and corrects your wrist by a finger's width.

choices.text: Say nothing, and ring the closing chime

effects.log: The chime is soft and clear. The voice ends mid-word, the way a candle is pinched.

events.text: You lay {gj9_name} to rest at the foot of a plum tree on a quiet isle, with the right words, in the right order. The yellow script is burned in a brass bowl. The bell is wrapped in a clean cloth. {gj9_title}. The tree has no blossoms, but a single bird, the first in years, lands on the lowest branch, and watches.

choices.text: Leave a cup of tea at the foot of the tree

effects.log: The cup is empty by morning, though no animal comes near. You do not tell anyone.

choices.text: Walk home without looking back

effects.log: You do not look back. The walk is shorter than you expected, and the bell weighs nothing.

events.text: It is done. The courtyard is quiet; the script is ash. {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}, lies where you laid them, with a stone at the head. Your disciples bring tea in the morning, and none of them ask what happened. One of them, the youngest, puts a white flower on the stone and looks at you, and you nod.

choices.text: Teach your disciples the closing words, for their own good

effects.log: You teach them. It takes a winter, and by spring it is the most honest thing your hall has ever done.

choices.text: Keep the stone in view of your window

effects.log: You keep it. On quiet evenings you raise a cup to it, and the evenings are the better for it.

events.text: A star falls slowly in the day sky and settles at the door of your temple as a figure in a robe of ash. {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}. You unseated them from the Nine's roll, not so long ago as gods count it. "A duel to the end," they say, without heat. "The Book of Fates has a page we are both on. One of us should finish it."

choices.text: Accept, and set the ground at the Edge of Domains

effects.log: You name the Edge. They bow, and the ground rearranges itself around the two of you, all the way to the sky.

choices.text: Refuse, and open your temple to them as a guest

effects.log: You open the gate. They look at the threshold, then at the lamp on it, and decline with a nod. The star goes up again.

events.text: The Hall of Lesser Heavens falls silent as {gj9_name} enters it without a herald. {gj9_title}. They do not speak to the gods who gather. They walk to the dais, place a white feather on it, and say, to you alone: "At dawn, on the star-road you took from me." Then they walk out, and the hall remains silent for a while.

choices.text: Pick up the feather, and take the star-road at dawn

effects.log: You pick it up. At dawn the road is bare except for them, standing in the exact centre, still as a column.

choices.text: Send the feather back with a written word of respect

effects.log: The feather returns the next morning with a single character on it: "No." You do not know how to answer a no.

events.text: An old herald from a pantheon that has not been worshipped in an age comes to your temple with a scroll and bows low. "My lord," it says, to you, "my lord {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}, begs a final audience." It does not say which of you the lord is. It says only that the audience will be over before the lamp at your gate burns down.

choices.text: Accept the audience, and light the gate lamp

effects.log: You light it. A figure walks up the star-road in the amber light, and the audience begins without a word.

choices.text: Say there is nothing to be settled between you

effects.log: The herald bows. It carries the answer back, and the answer, delivered, seems to go on being carried.

events.text: The Book of Fates, open on your altar, adds a line by itself: a duel is owed. The ink is still wet. {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}, has appealed to the oldest rule, that what ends one god may be asked for by another. Your heralds do not speak. The lesser gods drift to the temple eaves to watch. Nobody is in any doubt about how it will go on the star-road.

choices.text: Answer the line with your own, and go to meet it

effects.log: You write: "Granted." The ink dries, and the star-road, which had a moment ago been empty, has a figure on it.

choices.text: Cross the line out, and offer an apology in its place

effects.log: The line stays. Your apology sits beneath it, small, in a clear hand, and no one comes to read it.

events.text: {gj9_name} falls, and the star-road dims where they fell. {gj9_title}. A hush crosses the pantheons like a draught through a house. The Nine have one fewer, and the gods who built their quiet on that chair feel it go. Your own temple bells are silent, and your heralds, when they come, do not know how to greet you.

choices.text: Lay a single lamp on the star-road where they fell

effects.log: The lamp burns for a century, or seems to. Gods passing it slow their step, and some bow.

choices.text: Take their domain's blessing into your keeping, to guard

effects.log: The blessing is cold and sacred. It sits in your temple like a held breath, and your faith, oddly, rises.

events.text: It was never going to be a loud ending. {gj9_name} sits down on the star-road when it is over, as if tired, and does not rise. {gj9_title}. A thin rain falls from nowhere on the stones around them, and the lesser gods in the eaves look away. Somewhere beyond the sky a bell rings, once, for the Nine.

choices.text: Close their eyes with your own hand

effects.log: It is a small gesture, and the star-road is quiet for it. Your hand takes a day to warm.

choices.text: Walk to the end of the road and look at what is there

effects.log: There is nothing, and then there is a view. You see, for the first time, the edge of what you have won.

events.text: {gj9_name} lies in a quiet corner of the star-road, in a grave that pilgrims still tend. The stone says {gj9_title}, and no more. Faith lingers there, thin and sweet as smoke. In your sleeve the Corpse-Commanding Talisman has begun to warm, and the bell, silent since the burial, hums.

choices.text: Write the yellow script, and ring the bell

effects.log: You write and ring. The faith in the air turns, like milk, from sweet to something stranger.

choices.text: Leave before the pilgrims see you

effects.log: You leave. The pilgrims look up, find the road empty, and go back to their prayers, unsettled.

choices.text: Burn a full measure of incense, and close the grave to all hands

effects.log: The incense burns straight and long. Whatever stirred beneath the stone settles, and does not stir again.

events.text: On a lonely star, three heralds from the fallen pantheon keep a vigil over a mound of bright dust. {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}. They leave when they see you and do not come back. The dust gathers itself, softly, into a shape. In your sleeve the bell, with a clear little note, offers you a conversation.

choices.text: Take the bell and answer it in kind

effects.log: You ring. The dust rises, shaping a figure with its head bowed, its robe the colour of ash, its knees unbent.

choices.text: Cover the mound with a cloth and go

effects.log: The cloth settles, and for a time the dust does not move. You do not look back at it.

choices.text: Scatter salt and sing the closing hymn, once

effects.log: You sing. The dust sinks, and the star it lay on seems, for a moment, somewhat brighter.

events.text: The Book of Fates, as you pass it, turns a page for you with a dry rustle. It shows the grave of {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}, and a note in the margin in your own hand that you do not remember writing: "Ready." It is a simple word, and it carries a good deal of weight. Your bell is already half out of its cloth.

choices.text: Go to the grave, as the margin says

effects.log: You go. The grave knows you, and the earth lifts, a little, as a door lifts when a long-awaited guest knocks.

choices.text: Strike the margin note from the Book

effects.log: You strike it. The Book lets you, with a certain resigned air. The grave goes on lying where it is.

choices.text: Seal the grave with a god's own seal, and bind the Book too

effects.log: The seal burns your palm for a day. The Book is closed on that page, and the page does not open again.

events.text: What rises from the star-road grave is a Husk of a Fallen God, wrapped in yellow script, hollow where a presence used to be. {gj9_name} stands in the temple's outer court, upright, without bending a knee. {gj9_title}. The lesser gods fall silent, and your heralds, in a line, look at their own hands. The bell, in your grip, is nearly too cold to hold.

choices.text: Ring once, softly, to test its obedience

effects.log: It turns, slowly, and bows to the bell. It has done this before, to a bell far greater than yours.

choices.text: Stand a lamp at its feet, and watch the night through

effects.log: The lamp burns clear. The Husk does not blink, as there is nothing in it to blink. You are very awake, and it is grateful, or something like it.

events.text: On the first night it only stands. On the second it follows your shadow at a distance of three paces, wherever you walk the temple. On the third it stops at the door of the Hall of Fates and does not go in. {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}. You understand that it once stood at that door in another capacity, and that some courtesies outlive their givers.

choices.text: Open the Hall for it, and let it look in

effects.log: It looks in, a long while, and returns to your side. Whatever it came to see, it has seen.

choices.text: Lead it away, west, and shut the Hall door

effects.log: You do. It follows, jerky and obedient, and the Hall door shuts behind with a sigh like a held breath.

events.text: The bell rings by itself at the dead of the star-night, three times. When you reach the outer court the lid of the star-coffin lies on the stones and {gj9_name} stands facing the road, unbent. {gj9_title}. It is not waiting for the bell. It is remembering a domain, and the way to it, and the sky has gone very still.

choices.text: Ring the bell and hold it with all your will

effects.log: You ring and hold. The script glows, the stance loosens, and it turns back to you like a tide.

choices.text: Paste the sealing script on its brow, and lay it down for good

effects.log: The sealing script goes on. It stands a moment, then bows, then lies down by itself.

choices.text: Open the temple gate and let it go where it is going

effects.log: It goes through the gate without turning. The star-road bends once to take it, and then is empty.

events.text: Faith, in your temple, has begun to curdle. The offerings left for you turn grey on the altar overnight, and the prayers come in a lower register. {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}, stands in the central court, and where it stands the stone is rimed with frost. Your script on its forehead has gone the colour of old paper, and it is peeling.

choices.text: Rewrite the script in fresh cinnabar and ring it hard

effects.log: The new script drinks. The frost recedes. The Husk, stiffly, drops its head, and the offerings on the altar turn gold again.

choices.text: Sing the closing hymn and lay it in the ground yourself

effects.log: You dig with your own hands. It lies down in the grave, and you cover it, and neither of you speaks.

choices.text: Cut the old script away, and let the Husk be what it was

effects.log: The script comes away. It stands a moment as itself, and then it goes, and the court is just a court.

events.text: It is gone from the court when you wake, and the bell lies on the stones, cracked across. The track of frost leads out to the star-road, and along it, and past the edge of your domain. {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}, is walking toward the oldest temple in the sky, the one that was theirs. It does not look back. Your script is still on its brow, fading.

choices.text: Follow, ring the cracked bell, and call it back

effects.log: You follow it for nine days. At the oldest temple you ring, and it turns, as a sleepwalker does when named.

choices.text: Follow, and lay it down on the threshold of the oldest temple

effects.log: You follow. It reaches the threshold and stops. You lay it down gently, and it does not rise again.

choices.text: Let it walk on to the temple, and stand at a distance

effects.log: It reaches the door and passes in. The door closes. You wait there a long while, and nothing comes out.

events.text: Three pantheons have sent their heralds. A proclamation hangs in the Hall of Lesser Heavens in star-ink: whoever raised {gj9_name}, once one of the Nine Above, has defiled a seat of the gods. Tonight a delegation stands at your temple gate, carrying lanterns and a writ from the Book of Fates, and politely asks for the Husk.

choices.text: Receive the delegation in the court, beside the Husk

effects.log: You receive them. The Husk stands. After an hour of formal speech, the heralds go home with nothing, and with a great deal to report.

choices.text: Move the Husk to a hidden star by night

effects.log: You move it by night, along a star-road no one maps. The delegation finds a clean temple and a closed door.

events.text: The gods of three pantheons meet in closed session. Word of it reaches you the usual way, through a lesser god with a nervous cough: the matter before them is you, and a Husk, and the proper penalty. A herald with a writ is already on the star-road. The cough, as it leaves, says, "I'd not like to be you." It does not sound unkind.

choices.text: Go to the closed session, and speak for yourself

effects.log: You go. They hear you, stiffly. The ruling is deferred. It is the best you could have wished, and the worst thing that could be said of it.

choices.text: Go quiet for a century, and let the matter cool

effects.log: A century is a long time and no time at all. The matter cools, mostly, and is not entirely forgotten.

events.text: A herald you trust, one of your oldest, comes to you in the night and speaks quickly: the Nine have named a hunter, a god of silent roads. It has your Husk's scent, and your own. It will come within the season. "I would run," says the herald, "but I was never very brave. I would like to have run with you."

choices.text: Stay in your temple and wait for the hunter openly

effects.log: You wait. The hunter arrives, looks at you, at the Husk, at the gate, and for a long time says nothing. Then, to your surprise, it sits.

choices.text: Take your herald and go, swiftly, by the quiet road

effects.log: You go together. The quiet road is long and the herald talks the whole way, and it is a good, ragged, necessary talk.

events.text: You wake to find {gj9_name} standing over your altar, perfectly still, in the stance that began the last form of its art. It has never moved without the bell. {gj9_title}. The stance is beautiful. It is also aimed, with great precision, at the place where your temple's heart would be, and the lamps have all gone low.

choices.text: Watch the form to its end, without moving

effects.log: It completes the form. It is the best you have ever seen, and when it is done, it bows to you as an equal.

choices.text: Speak the closing hymn, and lay it to rest

effects.log: You say it. The Husk unbends slowly, as if grateful for the cue, and is still.

events.text: The Husk speaks, without the bell. One word, perhaps two, from a throat long past breathing: a name, the one a god would not speak aloud. {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}, looks at you with something that is nearly recognition. "You," it says, and something about a promise made on the star-road at the founding of the first temple.

choices.text: Ask what the promise was, and wait for the answer

effects.log: It does not answer. But it holds your eye a long moment, and you feel the oddest sense of being forgiven.

choices.text: Say the closing hymn before it can say more

effects.log: You say it, quickly, a little ashamed. It bows its head, and the court fills with the smell of rain.

events.text: Late in the night the voice of the Husk comes from the court: "Do you remember the second prayer?" It is {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}, in the tone of the god who first taught that prayer to you, in an age before your own. There is no malice in it. It is a question asked across a table, by a god who forgot it was dead.

choices.text: Answer, and speak the second prayer aloud

effects.log: You speak it. The Husk speaks with you, a half-beat behind, and corrects a single word in the middle.

choices.text: Say nothing, and ring the closing chime

effects.log: The chime is soft and clear. The voice ends mid-word, the way a candle is pinched.

events.text: You lay {gj9_name} to rest in a hollow of the star-road, with the right words in the right order. The yellow script is burned in a brass bowl. {gj9_title}. A star, small and white, comes out where there was none, and the lesser gods who see it from their eaves take off their crowns. For a moment the whole sky is courteous.

choices.text: Leave a cup of the thousand-year wine at the hollow

effects.log: The cup is empty by morning, though no god comes near. You tell no one.

choices.text: Walk home along the star-road without looking back

effects.log: You do not look back. The walk is shorter than you thought, and the bell weighs nothing.

events.text: It is done. The outer court is quiet; the script is ash. {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}, lies in the earth of your domain with a stone at the head and a lamp lit on it. Your heralds bring offerings, and none of them ask what happened. The youngest brings a white flower and looks at you, and you nod.

choices.text: Teach your heralds the closing hymn, for their own good

effects.log: You teach them. It takes a long winter, and by spring it is the most honest rite your temple has known.

choices.text: Keep the stone in view of your altar

effects.log: You keep it. On quiet nights you raise a cup to it, and the nights are the better for it.

events.text: A grey figure waits at the ferry stage of your river town, hat in hand, unhurried. {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}. You took their place on the list of the World's Ten not so long ago, in front of a good many people. "A duel to the end," they say, quite courteously. "Not for the list. For my pride, and I am sorry it is so small."

choices.text: Name the dry riverbed outside town, and go to meet them

effects.log: You name it. They nod, and the two of you walk out together while the ferrymen politely look away.

choices.text: Refuse, and offer them a seat and a pot of tea

effects.log: You offer the tea. They look at it for a long time, and decline, and the ferry takes them across.

events.text: A summons is nailed to the door of your house in the magistrate's neat hand, with a seal that is not the magistrate's: {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}, calls you to a last meeting at the old mill, at dawn, by the custom of the World's Ten. The magistrate has added, below, a small note that the town will not intervene. The note is not unkind.

choices.text: Go to the old mill at dawn, as written

effects.log: You go. The mill-wheel is still, the water stands, and the grey figure is already there, waiting without impatience.

choices.text: Write to decline, politely, and send gifts to the mill

effects.log: The gifts come back untouched. The note on top says only: "Another time." You suspect there is not one.

choices.text: Go the night before, and sit in the mill till dawn

effects.log: You sit in the mill all night. At first light they arrive, see you, and almost smile. It is nearly kind.

events.text: You find a pressed willow leaf in your ledger, which in the League's old custom is the mark of one who will not be refused. {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}. They are sitting on the low wall of your orchard, straight-backed, coat brushed, as if for a portrait. "I did not come to take it back," they say. "I came to finish it properly."

choices.text: Fetch your blade and walk out to meet them

effects.log: You walk out. The orchard is very quiet, and the two of you bow before you do anything else.

choices.text: Tell them it is finished, and mean it

effects.log: They look at you, and for a moment the old face shows through. Then it is gone, and they are walking off down the lane.

events.text: There is a note slipped under your door in the night, in the cramped handwriting of someone who does not often write. "The Lantern Bridge. Three nights. Come alone." It is signed {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}. Your neighbours have heard, as neighbours do, and every window on your street is lit, and every curtain just ajar.

choices.text: Cross the Lantern Bridge on the third night

effects.log: The bridge is hung with lanterns for a festival nobody remembers declaring. Halfway across, a lone figure turns to face you.

choices.text: Stay home, and let the lanterns burn without you

effects.log: The lanterns burn all night. In the morning the bridge is bare, the lanterns taken down, the street silent.

choices.text: Go early, and light the lanterns yourself

effects.log: You light them one by one. When they arrive, the bridge is bright, and they stand in the first lantern's glow and just look at it.

events.text: {gj9_name} does not get up. The mill-race runs on, the sky stays blue, and the nearest dog barks twice and stops. {gj9_title}. The kingdoms will hear by the first market day. You stand a while with your sword wiped and sheathed, listening for an old voice, and there is none.

choices.text: Close their eyes, and say the words for travellers

effects.log: You do it properly. A little of the weight lifts, as if the old words were a coin laid in a hand.

choices.text: Take their walking-stick, and leave the rest

effects.log: The stick is plain and worn at the grip. You will carry it for years, and it will not feel like a prize.

events.text: They lie with their face to the sky, hat beside them. The river town will want a ceremony; the League's Wardens will want a report; the road will want a story, and will make up what it needs. A single willow leaf lands on their coat from nowhere in particular. You could swear you hear someone hum.

choices.text: Carry them to the churchyard of a nearby village for burial

effects.log: They are buried under a plain stone, in a village that will sweep it each spring. You keep the village's name.

choices.text: Leave the body to the Wardens and walk away

effects.log: The Wardens take it with proper ceremony. You are not asked to the ceremony, and are, on the whole, glad.

events.text: {gj9_name} lies in a hillside churchyard above a river village that still sweeps the grave each spring. The stone says only {gj9_title}. Paper streamers move in no wind. In your sleeve the Corpse-Commanding Talisman is warm, and the little bell, silent since the burial, is trying to ring on its own.

choices.text: Write the yellow script and ring the bell

effects.log: You write the script. The earth turns once, like a sleeper, and the grass above it flattens.

choices.text: Leave before the villagers see you

effects.log: You leave quietly. Behind you the streamers stop all at once, like something that has been told to wait.

choices.text: Burn incense, and seal the grave for good

effects.log: The incense burns straight. You lay a stone upon the stone, and the bell in your sleeve goes quiet and cold.

events.text: A carter you hire for a fair price takes you, unasked, to the lane where {gj9_name} was laid. {gj9_title}. He will not meet your eye. The grave is a tidy little mound with a pear tree growing out of it, which should not be there, because it was not planted. The bell sings once, low, from your sleeve.

choices.text: Write the yellow script beneath the pear tree and ring

effects.log: The tree sheds all its blossom at once, in a long breath, and the mound begins to rise.

choices.text: Turn the cart around and go home

effects.log: The carter is visibly relieved. The pear tree watches the cart go, and does not bloom again that year.

choices.text: Set a second stone, and say the closing words

effects.log: You say them slowly. The pear tree gives a faint sigh and holds still. The bell is quiet from that day.

events.text: At the hour of the ox the bell on your wall speaks without a hand: one note, cold and very clear, and a direction. It points to the grave of {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}. You can feel the old art stirring there, patient, a sleeper turning toward warm voices. The yellow script in your pocket curls slightly at the edge, as paper does near a flame.

choices.text: Go to the grave, and answer the bell

effects.log: You go. At the grave you do not speak a word; you only write, and ring. The earth listens.

choices.text: Muffle the bell in a wet cloth and bury it a while

effects.log: You bury the bell in the garden. For a week the herbs above it lean north, and then they stop.

choices.text: Take salt, a lamp and an oath to the grave, and close it

effects.log: The salt makes a ring, the lamp burns steady, and the oath holds. The grave sleeps on, undisturbed.

events.text: What rose from the grave of {gj9_name} did not bend its knees to rise. It stands in your yard, a Walker of Your World, taller than a mortal should be, wrapped in yellow script, with a face composed in an old courtesy. {gj9_title}. The bell has only to ring and it will turn. Your neighbours, who know better, have bolted their doors.

choices.text: Ring once, softly, to learn if it still obeys

effects.log: It turns, with a creak like a gate in cold air, and bows. It has done this before, to better masters.

choices.text: Light a lamp at its feet and leave it standing till dawn

effects.log: It stands until dawn without a tremor. You do not sleep, and neither, in a way, does it.

events.text: The first night, it only stands. The second, it takes three steps and stops. On the third it turns toward the north road, where the river bends toward the League's old hall, and stays there until the bell makes it look away. {gj9_name}, you think. {gj9_title}. It remembers something, even now.

choices.text: Ring it to the south, away from the road

effects.log: It goes south, jerky and obedient, and the whole yard breathes out. You hold the bell harder than you meant to.

choices.text: Sit with it a while in the quiet, and ask nothing

effects.log: It does not answer. But for the length of one lamp's burning the air in the yard is a little less cold.

events.text: The bell rings by itself at midnight, three times. When you reach the shed the coffin lid is on the floor and {gj9_name} stands in the lane, facing the road, unbent. It is not waiting for your bell. It is remembering the way to somewhere, {gj9_title}. The yellow script has begun to curl at its edges like a leaf in fire.

choices.text: Ring the bell and hold it with your whole will

effects.log: You ring and ring. The script uncurls, the arms drop, and it turns back to you like a tide.

choices.text: Paste a sealing script on its back and lay it down for good

effects.log: The sealing script goes on. It stands a moment, then bows, then lies down by itself.

choices.text: Open the gate, and let it go where it is going

effects.log: It goes through the gate without turning. Somewhere down the river road a lamp is lit for it, or you imagine so.

events.text: Your bell is cracked. Hairline, but the note is wrong, like a voice carrying a thing it can no longer hold. {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}, has begun to move in the night on its own, a step at a time, always toward the old road. Two nights ago it reached the garden gate. This morning it stands in the doorway of your bedroom.

choices.text: Mend the bell with fresh script and ring it hard

effects.log: The new script blazes and drinks. The bell clears. The figure at the door steps back one pace and bows its head.

choices.text: Stand in the doorway yourself and say the closing words

effects.log: You say them. It listens, wholly still, to the very end. Then it kneels, folded neat as paper.

choices.text: Step aside from the doorway, and let it walk

effects.log: It walks past you. The lane seems to bend, once, to take it. After a time you cannot hear the steps.

events.text: Hens will not lay in your yard any more. The milk sours by noon. The Walker stands in the cold herb bed at night, among the frost, and there is frost on the ground only where it has stood. {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}. Your script on its forehead has faded to the colour of old paper. It will not stay on much longer.

choices.text: Rewrite the script in fresh cinnabar and bind it again

effects.log: The ink is cinnabar and not what it sounds like. The Walker shudders, and the frost goes out of the herb bed.

choices.text: Sing the closing chant, and lay it in the ground yourself

effects.log: You dig the grave with your own hands. It lies down in it, and you cover it, and neither of you speaks.

choices.text: Cut the old script from its brow, and let it be what it was

effects.log: The script comes away. It stands a moment as itself, and gives a nod that is nearly a bow.

events.text: Notices hang at every ferry stage in the kingdoms now, under a line in red: whoever raised {gj9_name}, once of the World's Ten, has robbed the League's own dead. Tonight a band of Wardens and three priests of the river shrine surround your house, lanterns up, and ask for the Walker in the name of the League of Kingdoms.

choices.text: Stand your ground beside the Walker, bell in hand

effects.log: You stand. The Wardens waver, and the priests recite, and the Walker does not move. After a long hour they withdraw.

choices.text: Slip away by the back lane and let them search an empty house

effects.log: You slip away. They find an empty house and one cold bell, which they dutifully carry off.

events.text: A letter, unsigned, from a Warden you once shared a boat with: they know. The League has met in closed session, and a magistrate is already on the road with a writ and a cart. It is kindly written and entirely clear. "I would not," the Warden adds, in the margin, "like to see how you answer it."

choices.text: Receive the magistrate openly, and argue your case

effects.log: You argue it. The magistrate is polite and unmoved, but leaves without the Walker, and with a great deal to report.

choices.text: Send the Walker downriver in a covered barge and clear your yard

effects.log: The Walker goes downriver at an unfashionable hour. The magistrate finds your yard swept, and blinks.

events.text: The ferryman at the lowest stage will not take your coin. He says, in a very low voice, that three Wardens were by, asking about a figure in yellow script at a certain house. He does not ask if it is true. He presses a bag of dried pears into your hand and says he has seen worse things end well.

choices.text: Go home and prepare your house for a visit

effects.log: You prepare. When they come, they find the house in order and the Walker at rest, and an argument is made on solid ground.

choices.text: Move the Walker at night, and shut the gate

effects.log: You move it by night, in a covered cart, at an unfashionable hour. The Wardens come at dawn to a locked gate and a swept yard.

events.text: You wake to find {gj9_name} standing over your bed, perfectly still, in the stance that began the last form of its art. It has never moved without the bell. The stance is beautiful. {gj9_title}. It is also, very faintly, aimed at you, and the house has gone as quiet as the river at midnight.

choices.text: Watch the form to its end, without moving

effects.log: It finishes the form. It is the best you have ever seen, and when it is done, it bows to you as to an equal.

choices.text: Speak the closing words and lay the figure to rest

effects.log: You say them. The figure unbends slowly, as if grateful for the cue, and is still.

events.text: The bell has not rung, but the Walker speaks. One word, perhaps two, from a throat that has not breathed in years: a name, the one you do not use. {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}, looks at you with something that is nearly recognition. "You," it says, and then something about a promise made on a ferry, in a year you cannot remember.

choices.text: Ask what the promise was, and wait for an answer

effects.log: It does not answer. But it holds your eye a long moment, and you have the oddest feeling of being forgiven.

choices.text: Say the closing words before it can say more

effects.log: You say them, quickly, a little ashamed. It bows its head, and the room fills with the smell of rain.

events.text: In the cold small hours a voice you almost know says, from the yard, "Do you remember the second step?" It is {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}, in the voice of the one who taught that step to you on a river-town quay, a long time ago. There is no malice in it. It sounds like a question asked across a table.

choices.text: Answer, and show the second step

effects.log: You show it. The Walker mirrors you, slowly, without a sound, and corrects your wrist by a finger's width.

choices.text: Say nothing, and ring the closing chime

effects.log: The chime is soft and clear. The voice ends mid-word, the way a candle is pinched.

events.text: You lay {gj9_name} to rest at the foot of a pear tree on a quiet hillside, with the right words in the right order. The yellow script is burned in a brass bowl. The bell is wrapped in a clean cloth. {gj9_title}. The tree has no blossom, but a single bird, the first in years, lands on the lowest branch, and watches.

choices.text: Leave a cup of tea at the foot of the tree

effects.log: The cup is empty by morning, though no animal comes near. You do not tell anyone.

choices.text: Walk home without looking back

effects.log: You do not look back. The walk is shorter than you expected, and the bell weighs nothing.

events.text: It is done. The yard is quiet; the script is ash. {gj9_name}, {gj9_title}, lies where you laid them, with a stone at the head. Your neighbours bring bread in the morning, and none of them ask what happened. The youngest brings a white flower for the stone and looks at you, and you nod.

choices.text: Teach the village children the closing words, for their own good

effects.log: You teach them. It takes a winter, and by spring it is the most honest thing the village has ever done.

choices.text: Keep the stone in view of your window

effects.log: You keep it. On quiet evenings you raise a cup to it, and the evenings are the better for it.
